evaluation.positioning_hook: A WNBA star returns to her Missouri hometown to bury her grandparents’ ashes in the town where they fell in love, and finds a new life — and a new love — in the man who helps her do it.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is clear and accessible: grief, second chances, and a sports heroine rebuilding her life. The market is narrower than a broad studio crowd because the script is intimate, faith-tinged, and more romance-forward than event-driven.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands cleanly once the story shifts from Skylar’s basketball arc to the Pottsville burial promise and Ralph connection. The opening championship material is vivid, but the actual feature engine takes a while to reveal itself.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Skylar has a strong, playable contradiction: elite competitor, grieving granddaughter, and woman relearning how to live off the court. Ralph is quietly compelling as a grounded caretaker, and Maddie gives the story a warm family anchor.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The blend of women’s basketball, funeral promise, and small-town romance gives the script a distinct lane. The execution is familiar in its emotional beats, though the setting and sports specificity help it stand apart.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script has several strong emotional turns, but it plays in long, reflective scenes and repeated relationship conversations. The burial journey and the romance move the story, yet the momentum is more contemplative than propulsive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The ashes-return premise gives the story a memorable spine, and the church/cemetery world adds a specific emotional texture. It feels fresh enough to remember, though not yet so singular that the premise alone sells itself.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Pottsville, the church, the school district, and the basketball culture create a coherent small-town ecosystem. The world is specific and usable, but it functions more as a warm container for the relationships than as a deeply layered system.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a consistent, sincere tone that leans into faith, family, and emotional uplift. It is recognizable and steady, though not especially hard-to-imitate or sharply stylized.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The Frank/Beth love story, Skylar’s injury, and Ralph’s guardedness suggest a deeper emotional life beneath the surface. The script hints at more than it fully dramatizes, which gives it some slow-burn appeal.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Skylar/Ralph/Maddie gives the feature a workable core triangle, and the family/church support system adds warmth. Still, the story is fundamentally carried by a few key relationships rather than a broad ensemble engine.

lead_characters.name: Skylar Monroe
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 20s; elite basketball player; Midwestern; emotionally guarded but warm; physically active lead.
lead_characters.hook: Skylar is a championship-level WNBA player who looks composed in public and unmoored in private. After a devastating injury and the loss of her grandfather, she comes home carrying ashes, grief, and a need to figure out who she is when basketball stops defining her; the role gives her a full arc from controlled star to vulnerable woman choosing a life, not just a career.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a Michelle Williams in Manchester by the Sea or a Brie Larson in Short Term 12 — a performance built on contained grief, physical stillness, and emotional release. It gives an actor the chance to play authority, collapse, and romantic awakening in one role.

lead_characters.name: Ralph
lead_characters.demographics: Man, early 40s; widowed father; church/school maintenance worker; working-class; emotionally restrained.
lead_characters.hook: Ralph is a steady, soft-spoken caretaker who has built his life around duty after loss. He’s the kind of man who fixes things before he talks about them, and the script uses that restraint as the emotional counterweight to Skylar’s upheaval; he becomes the quiet romantic center of the story without ever losing his grounded, lived-in quality.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of a Richard Jenkins in The Visitor or a Ben Mendelsohn in Leave No Trace — a restrained, emotionally legible man whose stillness carries real weight. It offers an actor the chance to play longing, decency, and late-blooming romantic risk without grand speeches.

lead_characters.name: Maddie
lead_characters.demographics: Girl, 8-14 across the story; Ralph’s daughter; basketball player; observant, earnest, emotionally open.
lead_characters.hook: Maddie is the story’s heart-on-sleeve observer, the kid who sees the adults more clearly than they see themselves. She gives the feature its innocence and its generational bridge, moving from grieving child to young athlete to the one who helps bring Skylar into the family orbit.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young performer the emotional clarity of Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project — naturalism, curiosity, and the chance to land scenes with adults without feeling precocious. It’s a strong showcase for a young actor who can play wonder and hurt in the same breath.

lead_characters.name: Beth Rose
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, late 60s to 70s; grandmother; warm, faith-centered, emotionally articulate.
lead_characters.hook: Beth is the keeper of memory and meaning, the one who turns basketball, marriage, and burial into a single emotional continuum. She’s not just a supportive elder; she’s the script’s moral compass, the person whose final request sends Skylar back to Pottsville and gives the story its purpose.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actress the grace-note authority of June Squibb in Nebraska — warmth, wit, and the ability to make a few scenes feel like the emotional spine of the film. It’s a prestige supporting part with real audience affection.

lead_characters.name: Frank Rose
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 70s; grandfather; faith-filled, basketball-loving, quietly wise.
lead_characters.hook: Frank is the remembered patriarch whose voice keeps echoing through the film even after his death. He functions as the story’s emotional inheritance — the man whose lessons about timing, patience, and belief shape both Skylar’s game and the love story that follows.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the understated authority of Hal Holbrook in Into the Wild or Tom Skerritt in A River Runs Through It — a few scenes, but a lasting imprint. It’s a legacy part that can land hard with very little screen time.

lead_characters.name: Jason
lead_characters.demographics: Man, late 20s; Skylar’s ex; emotionally steady but increasingly frustrated.
lead_characters.hook: Jason is the relationship from Skylar’s old life, the one who wants to love her through the injury but can’t survive being shut out. He’s not a villain; he’s the cleanest expression of the life Skylar is leaving behind, and that makes him useful and painful in equal measure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded heartbreak of Paul Mescal in Aftersun’s emotional register or Adam Driver in Marriage Story’s quieter scenes — a man who has to lose with dignity. It’s a strong supporting turn if cast with someone who can play hurt without turning brittle.

lead_characters.name: Coach Wensil
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s; high school coach; blunt, practical, community-minded.
lead_characters.hook: Coach Wensil is the local authority figure who recognizes Skylar’s value and gives her a place to land. He’s a functional but useful supporting presence, especially in the school-gym material where the film starts to feel like a lived-in community story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid character-actor role in the lane of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Jeffrey Wright in a grounded ensemble — not flashy, but scene-stabilizing. It gives an actor the chance to play command, skepticism, and warmth in a few efficient beats.

lead_characters.name: Coach Green
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 50s; professional basketball coach; calm, commanding, team-first.
lead_characters.hook: Coach Green is the pro-level counterpart to the small-town coaches, the person who frames Skylar’s injury and comeback in the language of leadership. She’s efficient on the page, but she helps widen the world beyond Pottsville and keeps the basketball stakes credible.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong, contained authority role in the vein of Viola Davis in Fences’ command scenes or Octavia Spencer in a mentor mode — a chance to project competence and emotional intelligence quickly. It’s a good part for an actor who can make leadership feel lived-in.

lead_characters.name: Sharon Maid
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 40s; parish administrator; warm, organized, local connective tissue.
lead_characters.hook: Sharon is the practical face of the church world, the person who makes the burial promise feel administratively real rather than symbolic. She’s a small but useful bridge character who helps the town feel functional and humane.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded utility of a strong ensemble player in a Hallmark-adjacent or prestige-drama setting — efficient, specific, and believable. It’s not a showy part, but it has clean scene utility.

lead_characters.name: Father Phillips
lead_characters.hook: Father Phillips is the film’s spiritual sounding board, the man who gives the story its faith-based framing without turning it into sermonizing. He helps translate grief into ritual and gives Ralph and Skylar a moral language for the choices they’re making.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the quiet authority work of a Richard Jenkins or a David Strathairn type — measured, compassionate, and memorable without overplaying. It’s a prestige-supporting part for an actor who can make stillness feel active.

casting_characteristics: one athletic female lead with credible basketball skill
one child role that ages from 8 to 14 across the story
basketball team and crowd scenes require background casting

technical.vfx_details: Primarily scoreboard inserts, crowd enhancement, and possible cleanup/compositing for arena and game-day coverage.
technical.sfx_needs: Basketball game choreography, injury fall/stretcher handling, practical crowd and confetti moments.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: intimate, character-driven sports drama with romance and faith elements, best suited to streaming or specialty theatrical.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the championship-game arena material, crowd scenes, and multiple basketball sequences will require real production value to feel credible.

casting.note: Skylar needs a lead who can credibly play elite basketball and carry grief, romance, and authority; Maddie also needs a young performer who can age across the story.

development.note: The script’s emotional spine is clear, but the feature is built from a long series of reflective scenes and time jumps, so the buying conversation will focus on whether the burial journey and romance are enough to sustain the runtime.

comp_set.title: The Way Back
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-struck athlete rebuilding identity through sport and routine, with the emotional engine anchored in recovery rather than competition.

comp_set.title: The Blind Side
comp_set.why_it_comps: A sports story that uses family, faith, and community warmth to broaden the audience beyond basketball fans.

comp_set.title: A League of Their Own
comp_set.why_it_comps: Women’s basketball energy, team chemistry, and a sentimental crowd-pleaser lane built around female athletic identity.

comp_set.title: The Last Letter from Your Lover
comp_set.why_it_comps: The buried-love-story structure and dual emotional timelines echo the film’s romance-through-memory design.

comp_set.title: The Rookie
comp_set.why_it_comps: A faith-forward, family-friendly sports drama with uplift, community stakes, and a clean emotional payoff.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adult women and faith-friendly audiences who respond to emotional sports dramas, small-town romance, and family-centered uplift.
audience_target.demographics: 35+ skew, female-leaning, middle America and suburban viewers, plus sports-drama and inspirational-drama audiences.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary small-town settings keep the spend contained, but basketball arena scenes, crowd work, and a handful of travel/time-jump sequences push it above micro.

types_of_buyers: specialty distributors seeking inspirational adult dramas
streamer development teams building female-led uplift lanes
indie producers with access to sports-friendly locations
faith-adjacent buyers looking for clean emotional content
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in a warm, accessible lane where sports, grief, and romance can coexist without irony. The church/cemetery material and the basketball backbone make it legible to buyers who want emotional uplift with a clear audience promise.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the story resolves Skylar’s emotional arc and the Ralph/Skylar relationship without a clear sequel or universe vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The burial promise gives the film a clean engine.
strengths.what_it_means: That promise turns a character drama into a mission-based feature, which makes the story easier to market and easier to emotionally track. Buyers looking for a contained, audience-friendly hook will understand the movie immediately once the ashes journey is introduced.
strengths.evidence: Beth asks Skylar to return Frank and Beth’s ashes to Pottsville, and Skylar drives cross-country to make it happen.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Skylar is a credible star role.
strengths.what_it_means: The role combines athletic authority, grief, and romantic vulnerability, which is exactly the kind of part that can elevate a mid-level package. Casting directors and talent reps will see a showcase for an actress who can carry both physical confidence and emotional collapse.
strengths.evidence: She wins at the buzzer, tears down after the injury, and then slowly rebuilds her identity in Pottsville.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The church-and-school world feels lived in.
strengths.what_it_means: The setting gives the film a grounded, values-forward texture that broadens its appeal beyond sports fans. That makes the project easier to position to buyers who want a clean, emotionally legible world with recognizable institutions.
strengths.evidence: Ralph works at the church and school district, and the story repeatedly moves through the gym, cemetery, parish office, and family home.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The romance is earned through shared labor.
strengths.what_it_means: The Skylar/Ralph connection grows out of practical care — burial logistics, gym work, and parenting — which gives the relationship a sturdier commercial footing than a purely meet-cute romance. That makes it attractive to audiences who want intimacy with emotional credibility.
strengths.evidence: Ralph helps with the graves, takes Skylar to the cemetery, and later becomes the person she dances with at the spring event.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Maddie gives the film a family audience bridge.
strengths.what_it_means: The daughter role widens the emotional entry point and gives the story a younger point of identification without turning it into a kids’ movie. That helps the film play as a cross-generational family drama rather than a narrow adult romance.
strengths.evidence: Maddie watches Skylar’s games, reacts to the coaching, and becomes the bridge between Ralph’s home life and Skylar’s new one.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, emotionally legible feature with a strong female-lead showcase, a mission-based hook, and a contained small-town production footprint. The combination of sports credibility, faith-adjacent warmth, and a romance built from shared responsibility makes it easy to imagine for a streamer or specialty buyer looking for uplift without cynicism.

items.area: The opening championship material is a false start.
items.detail: The script spends a long stretch on Skylar’s basketball success before the actual feature engine — the ashes promise and Pottsville return — fully takes over. That makes the first act feel like a prologue to the real movie, which is a buying conversation risk because the hook arrives late.

items.area: The middle plays as a series of emotional beats.
items.detail: A lot of the feature is built from reflective conversations in the hospital, apartment, church, and cemetery rather than from escalating external turns. That gives the film sincerity, but it also means momentum depends heavily on performance and audience patience.

items.area: The basketball credibility narrows the casting pool.
items.detail: Skylar has to read as an elite pro athlete, not just a character who talks about basketball, and the script repeatedly puts her in game-action and leadership positions. That is a real casting lift for a mid-budget package, especially if the buyer expects the sports material to feel authentic.

items.area: The brand and league references need a legal pass.
items.detail: The script names the Phoenix Mercury, Indiana Fever, New York Liberty, NCAA, Notre Dame, University of Missouri, and Gainbridge Fieldhouse, which are all clearance items if kept as written. That is manageable, but it is not invisible, and it will matter in any greenlight conversation built around a clean rights package.

items.area: Jason functions more as a pressure device than a full rival.
items.detail: He’s useful as the life Skylar is leaving behind, but the script doesn’t give him enough independent texture to feel like a fully durable counterweight to Ralph. Buyers will notice that the romantic triangle is emotionally clear, but structurally it’s more about Skylar’s choice than about three equally forceful positions.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is structural: it takes time to get from the basketball prologue to the actual burial-and-romance engine, and much of the middle is carried by mood rather than escalation. The other producer-level conversations are practical — a demanding athlete casting lane and a non-trivial clearance pass on the named teams, league, and arena references.
